intro_html:
SB 157 died when the 30-day session ended on 19 February 2026, so a new bill would have to be filed for the session that opens in January 2027. In Albuquerque the utility is PNM, whose customer solar program runs through an online application, a technical review, and inspections and approvals before a system is connected, under 17.9.568 NMAC. Two details matter for a plug-in kit: since 29 March 2024 every application must specify an advanced inverter compliant with IEEE 1547-2018, and PNM’s FAQ says customers may do the work themselves if they are licensed electricians.

New Mexico’s solar-rights law is broad on paper. NMSA §3-18-32 voids any covenant, restriction or condition in an instrument affecting “the transfer, sale or use of, or an interest in, real property” that effectively prohibits a solar collector, and the Solar Rights Act defines a solar collector to include any device that collects solar energy for “the generation of electricity”. The Attorney General has read “effectively prohibit” to include rules that make installation unreasonably difficult or costly (Op. No. 11-02). Read literally, that could reach condominium rules about balconies. But SB 157 would have applied the same rule to plug-in devices by name, “pursuant to” §3-18-32, which suggests its sponsors did not regard the point as settled, and nothing in these statutes removes PNM’s interconnection requirements.

balco.nyc’s calculator models a specific Albuquerque address and lets you enter the rate from your own PNM bill in place of the state’s 15.3¢ average.

faq: Does New Mexico's solar rights law protect a balcony solar panel?

Possibly, but it is untested. NMSA §3-18-32 voids covenants and other real-property instruments that effectively prohibit a solar collector, and the Solar Rights Act defines a solar collector to include devices that generate electricity. SB 157 would have applied that rule to plug-in devices by name, suggesting the point was not considered settled, and none of it removes PNM’s interconnection requirements. This is not legal advice.
